810.bp: Organizations need to detect Advanced Persistent Threats—careful, multi-stage cyber attacks that stay hidden inside systems for months while stealing data or sabotaging infrastructure. Traditional security tools catch simple attacks, but APTs deliberately coordinate hundreds of small actions across different parts of a computer system to evade detection.
810.wh: Most threat detection tools only look at pairs of events (one thing connected to one other thing), which misses the crucial pattern in APTs: multiple system components working together in a single coordinated step. Also, attackers spread their work over time across a whole computer system, so detectors that only look at nearby neighbors miss the full picture of how an attack unfolds from stage to stage.
810.ap: HyperDetector models attack behavior as a hypergraph—a graph where a single connection can link many entities at once, just like a real system event might touch the file system, network, and memory simultaneously. It then uses a global attention mechanism (similar to how you might track a conversation by remembering both recent words and threads from the beginning) to connect distant parts of the hypergraph so the detector can see how an attack spreads across the whole system.
810.ww: By representing multi-entity actions as single hyperedges, the model naturally captures how APT actions coordinate—much more honest than forcing everything into pairs. The global attention helps because real attacks reveal themselves through patterns that span the whole system history, and the detector can now reason about those long-distance relationships instead of getting lost in local noise.
810.po: The approach achieves better detection of Advanced Persistent Threats by understanding both how multiple system parts collaborate in single operations and how those operations chain together across time, catching attacks that simpler pair-based methods miss.

811.bp: Deep learning systems that read or understand text—such as those used in content moderation, email filtering, or search—are vulnerable to adversarial attacks: tiny, crafted tweaks to input text that flip the output without humans noticing. Attackers want to fool these systems without needing to know how they work internally.
811.wh: Most adversarial attacks require access to the target system to test and refine the attack. But real-world systems are closed: a bank's fraud detector or a platform's moderation system won't let attackers probe them. Attackers instead must create attacks using a stand-in model they control, then hope those attacks still work on the real system (this is called transfer). Existing transfer methods treat all stand-in models equally or guess importance scores poorly, so attacks don't transfer as well as they could.
811.ap: SEP-Attack uses a mathematical tool called Determinantal Point Process to generate a diverse set of stand-in models weighted by how well each one's failures transfer to the real system. Then it scores each word by how much changing it hurts the stand-in ensemble's confidence, identifies candidate attacks, and ranks those candidates by their expected transferability before picking the best ones.
811.ww: By weighting stand-in models based on real transfer behavior rather than treating them equally, the method focuses on the failure modes most likely to fool the real system. The final transferability score acts as a sanity check: it measures whether changes that hurt the stand-in will actually fool the target, so the attack doesn't waste effort on tricks that won't transfer.
811.po: The method generates adversarial text that fools real-world APIs and closed systems significantly better than existing methods by modeling which failures actually transfer rather than guessing which stand-in models matter.

812.bp: Recommendation systems that suggest products, articles, or videos to users need to train on enormous amounts of data—user clicks, ratings, searches—which costs companies huge amounts of compute time and electricity. Selecting a smaller representative subset of that data could cut training time while keeping recommendation quality high.
812.wh: When you pick a small subset of data, you're exposed to a big problem: real-world user-item interactions are messy and full of noise. A user might click on something by accident, or data might be mislabeled. A small subset is especially vulnerable because any noise in it becomes a bigger fraction of the total signal. Also, the subset must actually be representative—it can't just be the 'easiest' or 'most obvious' examples or the model will learn narrow patterns.
812.ap: Noise-aware Coreset Selection uses gradient information to identify which data points are most valuable for training (via a technique called submodular optimization that balances coverage and informativeness). Simultaneously, it corrects labels on noisy examples by gradually training a model and checking which predictions are confident versus uncertain. Finally, it filters out unreliable interactions by discarding samples where the model is unsure.
812.ww: By correcting noisy labels and removing low-confidence samples before training on the subset, the method ensures the small training set has high-quality signal. The gradient-based selection ensures every kept sample contributes something unique to the model's learning, so even a tiny subset covers the full range of user behaviors the system needs to learn.
812.po: The system recovers 93–95% of performance from training on the full dataset while using only a fraction of the data and compute, by carefully removing noise and selecting only the most informative examples for content-based recommendation.

813.bp: Open source projects like Linux and Chromium shape the entire digital world, yet we lack good tools to understand whether communities building them are healthy—whether contributors stick around, whether they're collaborating effectively, whether the project will survive. GitHub hosts 100 million users, but existing measurement tools are too simple to capture the real dynamics of these communities.
813.wh: Most tools count surface metrics like 'how fast are pull requests reviewed' or 'how many stars did the project get this month,' but these numbers don't reveal how people actually work together or whether the community itself is robust. Also, different projects need different data points; no single fixed tool works for all questions. Current data collection is slow or limited, making it hard to study many projects or get fine-grained details.
813.ap: OpenDigger provides two parts: OpenCrawler, a customizable data collector that can pull whatever specific information you need from open source platforms at fine granularity, and OpenDigger itself, which computes both statistical metrics (like contributor churn or issue resolution time) and network-based metrics (like how clustered or central different contributors are in the collaboration graph).
813.ww: Network metrics reveal whether a community is fragmented into isolated groups or connected through hub maintainers—a sign of health not captured by simple counts. By making data collection flexible, the system lets researchers ask new questions and spot problems specific to different project types, whether that's a library, an application, or an infrastructure project.
813.po: The framework enables multi-dimensional assessment of open source project health and collaboration patterns, moving beyond activity counts to reveal whether communities are sustainable and well-connected.

814.bp: Large language models are now used to re-rank search results—taking a huge list of candidates and reordering them by quality to show the best results first. But LLMs are slow: they process text one piece at a time (auto-regressive decoding), which creates a bottleneck in ranking, making real-time search expensive.
814.wh: The standard way LLMs generate output is one step at a time, and for ranking, that means considering each position in the result list one by one. This is necessary in normal text generation (you can't write the next word until you've written all previous words), but ranking doesn't have that dependency—you could theoretically score multiple orderings in parallel. Naive attempts to skip steps lose accuracy, especially for items ranked last, because the model's predictions depend on knowing which items came before.
814.ap: ONE-PASS uses a clever observation: the model's next prediction doesn't depend heavily on the exact order of previous items, only which items are there. This lets the system reduce the explosive number of possible orderings (N factorial) down to combinations (2^N). It then divides the full ranking into K chunks and scores each chunk independently, reducing the space further. Finally, it uses Möbius inversion—a mathematical technique for decomposing how parts contribute to a whole—to correctly combine chunk scores into a full ranking.
814.ww: By treating partial orderings rather than exact permutations, the method cuts computation from factorial to exponential, making it tractable. Möbius inversion is the key because it correctly weights how subsets of items interact—it prevents the naive approach's problem of double-counting or missing item dependencies when combining chunk probabilities.
814.po: The system ranks lists in a single forward pass through the model while keeping accuracy—cutting inference time dramatically compared to auto-regressive item-by-item ranking, making LLM-based re-ranking practical at production scale.

815.bp: Cell phone users in Korea and elsewhere depend on centralized identity systems to access banking, healthcare, and government services. But these systems are risky: if a company's servers are breached (as happened to SK Telecom in 2025, affecting 23 million people), attackers can steal identity data from everyone at once. A decentralized approach could eliminate that single point of failure.
815.wh: Today's systems work like this: you prove who you are to a company, and they vouch for you to other services. But that company becomes a target, and if compromised, all its credentials are exposed. Decentralized alternatives have existed but are slow, expose private keys during authentication, or don't meet real-time speed requirements for practical use.
815.ap: This system gives each person a decentralized identifier (a cryptographic key pair) stored only on their device, never on a company's server. When proving identity, the person uses Schnorr signatures and zero-knowledge proofs—mathematical techniques that prove 'I know a secret' without ever revealing the secret itself. The system follows W3C standards for verifiable credentials so it works across different services.
815.ww: Zero-knowledge proofs let you prove you are who you claim without handing over proof that could be stolen or reused. By building on the mathematical difficulty of the discrete logarithm problem (the same hard math that secures Bitcoin), the system gets strong cryptographic security without needing a trusted company in the middle. Decentralization means there's no database to breach.
815.po: The system authenticates users for real-time services (signature in under 10 ms, verification under 15 ms) while keeping their private keys secure and eliminating dependence on centralized carriers, closing the security gap that exposed 23 million Koreans in 2025.

816.bp: Every day, people share their thoughts, conversations, and personal details on social media. These texts are now harvested to train AI language models, but the people posting rarely consent or realize their private information is being used to teach machines. Some of those machines might later leak or misuse that information.
816.wh: Obvious secrets like 'my phone number is 555-1234' can be blanked out, but real privacy leaks are subtle and hide in context. Someone might never mention their home address directly but say 'I take the 7:40 AM train from the corner near my apartment'—from that sentence, someone could infer which town they live in. Detecting these implicit leaks requires understanding what clues in the text could let an attacker reverse-engineer private information.
816.ap: PrivSniffer models each piece of user text as a graph where words and phrases are nodes and meaning-based relationships are edges. It then combines the reasoning power of a large language model (which understands nuance) with precise graph search (which methodically finds chains of clues). For each sensitive fact (like location), it searches for paths through the text where clues connect together to reveal that fact.
816.ww: Language models are good at intuition but can miss logical chains, while graph search is thorough but needs the right structure. By combining both, the system finds privacy leaks that either method alone would miss. The graph structure forces the model to explain *why* a leak exists—which clues led to the breach—making detection reliable.
816.po: The system detects contextual privacy leaks in user-generated text with 64% higher accuracy than previous methods (F1 of 0.59 versus 0.36), enabling practical text sanitization before personal writing is fed to AI training.

817.bp: When you watch short videos on TikTok or YouTube, the app tries to recommend videos you'll like. These recommendations work better if the system understands not just *which* videos you watched, but *when* you watched them and *how long* you spent on each—your pauses and dwell times reveal your changing moods and interests.
817.wh: Standard transformer models use 'positional encoding'—a way to tell the model 'this is the first item, this is the second item' so it knows sequence order. But they usually ignore *when* events happen or how long you spent on each. Time intervals between user actions (dwell time) contain real signal about whether someone is interested, bored, or distracted, but most systems just treat time as a number instead of as a pattern.
817.ap: TSAPE models time intervals not as raw numbers but as a sequence of patterns: it looks at whether intervals are getting longer or shorter, speeding up or slowing down. It then feeds these patterns through multiple layers of one-dimensional convolutional networks and attention mechanisms (which weight different time patterns by importance), blending this temporal signal into the normal positional encoding.
817.ww: Time intervals are meaningful as patterns (a user who spends 1 second then 2 seconds then 5 seconds is escalating interest, different from someone who does 5 then 2 then 1). By modeling the sequence of intervals rather than their raw values, the system captures the user's emotional trajectory. Convolutional layers find recurring time patterns, and attention weights lets the model learn which temporal patterns matter most for prediction.
817.po: The system improves sequential recommendation in short-video platforms by capturing evolving user interest through time patterns, enabling better predictions of what video a user will engage with next based on how their viewing behavior is changing.

818.bp: Specialized AI systems that handle medical diagnoses, legal research, or scientific discovery need real, up-to-date knowledge in their domain. Combining a language model with a knowledge graph (a structured map of facts) helps—but high-quality knowledge graphs are expensive and incomplete, requiring constant expert input to fix and expand.
818.wh: Language models sometimes 'hallucinate'—generating plausible-sounding but false answers. When you try to fix this by asking experts to correct the model and update the knowledge graph, you hit two problems: experts are expensive and time-consuming, and you're throwing away what the model already knows correctly. Most existing systems treat expert answers as fully correct and the model as fully unreliable, missing the chance to learn from what the model gets right.
818.ap: EC-spLLM teaches the language model to understand its own reliability through 'epistemic cognition'—knowing when to trust itself and when to defer to experts. When the model generates an answer, it checks whether hallucination is likely (by scoring internal consistency and searching for contradictions). Based on that self-assessment, the system either uses the expert's corrected answer *or* keeps the model's answer if confidence is high. This same choice mechanism improves the knowledge graph over time.
818.ww: By letting the model assess its own confidence, the system avoids wasting expert time on things the model already does well. Hallucination detection catches flaky outputs, so when the system trusts the model's answer, that answer is reliable. This bridges internal and external knowledge: experts fix critical mistakes, but the system reuses correct model outputs, reducing expert burden while building a better knowledge graph.
818.po: The framework reduces expert dependency for maintaining domain knowledge graphs while improving the specialized language model's performance across five domains by learning to distinguish reliable model reasoning from hallucinations.

819.bp: Companies sometimes collaborate by having each participant train a machine learning model on their own private data, then merging the models. This 'split learning' lets hospitals share a diagnostic model without revealing patient records. But split learning has a critical flaw: a malicious participant can poison their embeddings (the compressed representations they send) to sabotage the final model for everyone.
819.wh: In split learning, each participant sends numeric summaries (embeddings) to a central trainer, not raw data. A malicious participant can subtly alter these numbers—add a hidden trigger pattern—so that later, when the final model sees that trigger, it produces wrong answers. The problem is that poisoned embeddings look almost identical to clean ones, so a simple check won't catch them.
819.ap: SecureSplit stretches the embeddings into a higher-dimensional space where subtle differences magnify—poisoned and clean embeddings now stand out. It then uses a majority vote: if 7 embeddings say the image is a cat and 1 says it's a dog, the system trusts the 7 and discards the 1 poisoned embedding. This simple voting scheme is robust because honest participants outnumber attackers.
819.ww: Dimensionality transformation amplifies the signal of poisoning because malicious changes, while small, are systematic—they follow a pattern. Majority voting works because it's hard for an attacker to fool many independent models at once; one bad participant can't overpower many honest ones. The combination of magnification and voting catches most backdoor attempts without false positives.
819.po: The system defends split learning against backdoor attacks from malicious participants across four image datasets and five attack scenarios, preserving clean embeddings while filtering poisoned ones so collaborative training stays safe.

820.bp: AI agents—autonomous software systems that can browse the web, send emails, and coordinate with each other—are starting to operate across the open internet, discovering services, communicating, and negotiating without human intervention. Building standards and infrastructure for this 'Agentic Web' is crucial so millions of agents can interoperate safely and fairly.
820.wh: Right now, each AI agent is isolated: it runs on one company's servers and talks only to systems that company controls. For agents to work together across the web like humans do, they need common protocols (like HTTP but for agents), agreed-upon identity standards, and ways to prove they're trustworthy. There's also no clear way to handle reputation, payment, liability, or coordination at scale.
820.ap: This workshop brings together researchers and practitioners to explore how to build interoperable agent architectures—common standards and protocols that let any agent talk to any service. It covers cryptographic identity, economic mechanisms (how agents pay each other), governance (who enforces rules), and coordination (how agents find and trust each other).
820.ww: The Agentic Web mirrors the human web: humans cooperate through trust mechanisms (reviews, reputation), governance (laws, platforms), and standards (language, currency). Agents need the same infrastructure. By establishing foundations now, before millions of agents exist, the community can prevent fragmentation and lock-in later.
820.po: The workshop establishes a forum for defining technical interoperability, economic structures, and governance frameworks that will enable AI agents to operate as first-class entities on the web rather than isolated tools.

821.bp: Viral marketing campaigns try to pick a small set of 'seed' people to influence so that their friends talk about a product, and those friends' friends do too, creating a cascade. But companies rarely know the full friendship network—it might be hidden for privacy, incomplete, or constantly changing, so traditional influence-maximization algorithms fail.
821.wh: Influence-maximization methods rely on knowing the network structure: 'if I seed person A, B, and C, how many people will eventually hear about this?' But in real scenarios, the network is partially hidden. Also, real human behavior is complex: whether someone adopts an idea depends on who influenced them, *when* it happened, and subtle social dynamics that change over time. Predicting influence without explicit network structure is extremely hard.
821.ap: DynaFLUX learns hidden network dynamics directly from observed cascades—patterns in *when* people adopt things—without needing to see all the links. It uses a generative model to reverse-engineer what the network probably looks like based on timing patterns. For seed selection, it uses reinforcement learning with a pointer network (a neural technique for ordering items) to find which seed set will likely trigger the biggest cascade, using a reward signal from predicted influence.
821.ww: Timing carries information about network structure: if person A adopts something, then B adopts it moments later, they're probably connected. By learning hidden dynamics, the system doesn't need the explicit graph. The pointer network is good at finding optimal selections without checking all possible combinations (which would be computationally infeasible). Monte Carlo diffusion (sampling many cascade possibilities) gives noisy but real influence estimates that drive the learning process.
821.po: The system identifies influential seed nodes and consistently outperforms traditional methods in settings where the network is hidden, partial, or noisy—enabling viral campaigns without requiring knowledge of the full social graph.

822.bp: When you search on Google or another search engine, you form quick expectations about what's on the page based on the title and snippet—and when the page disappoints you (maybe the title was misleading), your attention disrupts and you leave frustrated. If search engines could detect these moments in real-time, they could fix snippets or show better results before users give up.
822.wh: Detecting disappointment in a search result is hard because it's invisible—you can't see it from the page content alone. Users might hover, scroll, then leave, which looks like normal browsing. The challenge is distinguishing 'I found what I wanted and I'm reading carefully' from 'this is wrong and I'm frustrated.' You need insight into how the user's attention is actually working, not just what they clicked.
822.ap: The study uses eye-tracking to measure where people look and for how long on disappointing versus satisfying search results. It measures four gaze metrics: how quickly they first look at the page, total time spent looking at it, how many times they glance at it, and average duration per glance. Machine learning models trained on these eye patterns predict whether the user experienced an expectancy violation.
822.ww: Expectancy violations show up in *sustained* attention (total time looking + number of glances) rather than immediate reflexive looks. This makes intuitive sense: if a page is wrong, people re-examine it trying to find what they're looking for, creating longer, more frequent looks. The result reveals that disappointment isn't an instant reflex—it's a deeper cognitive disruption showing up as engaged but confused eye behavior.
822.po: The system predicts expectancy violations during web search with 62.6% accuracy (well above random chance), enabling future search interfaces to detect real-time cognitive mismatches and offer corrective support before users abandon their search.

823.bp: Douyin and TikTok watch users clicking through short videos in rapid succession, and to recommend the next video well, they need to remember the last thousands of videos you watched. But keeping track of 10,000 previous videos in memory is computationally expensive—storage, compute time, and network costs explode. The challenge is honoring this long history without breaking latency (response time) or budget.
823.wh: Standard neural networks that handle sequences (like transformers) check how each item relates to every other item—a quadratic cost that becomes prohibitively expensive with 10,000 items. You could use older techniques that only look at recent history, but then you lose signal: maybe a user's interest changed 5,000 videos ago, and that's crucial to understanding them today. There's a tension between remembering long history and staying fast.
823.ap: The system uses three innovations: (1) Replace the expensive 'attend to everything' mechanism with 'attend from target to history'—the next-video recommendation only looks back to find supporting context, not bidirectional (this cuts complexity from quadratic to linear). (2) Batch multiple recommendations for the same user together so they share the encoded history, reusing computation. (3) Train the model on shorter 2,000-item windows but at inference time apply it to 10,000-item windows—this 'length extrapolation' lets it generalize without extra training cost.
823.ww: One-directional attention (from target backward to history) is sufficient because the model only needs to find relevant context, not map out all relationships. Batching exploits the fact that a user's long history doesn't change between consecutive recommendations. Length extrapolation works because the model learns position-relative patterns that generalize: if it learned 'look 100 steps back for interest signals,' it can apply that to 500 steps back.
823.po: The system deployed on Douyin handles 10,000-item user histories in production while meeting latency requirements and improving engagement metrics, demonstrating that long-sequence modeling scales when you replace global comparison with targeted history retrieval.

824.bp: Digital maps power navigation, delivery, and location search. As cars and delivery vehicles move through cities constantly, their GPS trajectories become valuable raw material for inferring or updating maps—cheaper than hiring surveyors. But inferring accurate road networks from trajectory traces is harder than it looks, especially in dense urban areas where roads overlap or lie close together.
824.wh: Most current systems convert trajectories into a rasterized image (a pixelated grid), then find corners and trace connections like an image-processing problem. But this loses information: multi-level roads (overpasses, tunnels) get flattened, and in dense downtown areas, nearby parallel roads blur together. Also, connecting corners often fails in dense areas where many roads cluster—the system can't tell which roads actually connect.
824.ap: D2Map uses two different representations of the same trajectory data at once: the rasterized image (standard, covers area well) and a serialized trajectory view (which explicitly shows which roads are traversable in sequence from the raw GPS traces). It learns how to intelligently combine these two views—sometimes trusting the image, sometimes trusting the trajectory order—through a learned fusion module. For building the map, it builds not just a primal graph (roads as nodes, connections as edges) but also a dual graph (intersections as nodes) and reasons about both together.
824.ww: The serialized trajectories preserve order—'vehicle went from road A to road B to road C'—which directly encodes adjacency. The image captures spatial density. Together they're complementary: the image finds structure in sprawl, the sequence fixes connectivity in clutter. Dual-graph reasoning (treating both roads and intersections as entities) prevents false connections by checking consistency: if two roads share an intersection in the primal graph, that must be reflected in the dual.
824.po: The system infers digital road maps from vehicle trajectories with higher topological accuracy in complex scenarios by reasoning over dual representations and learning when to trust spatial density versus traversal sequence.
